title: What an Operating System Does
summary: The operating system is the program that runs the computer for every other program - it shares the CPU and memory between programs, gives them files and devices through one safe interface, keeps them from interfering with each other, and starts and stops them. Its core, the kernel, is the only code allowed to touch the hardware directly.
markdown:
## The program that runs the programs Turn on a computer with no operating system and you get a CPU fetching instructions from memory - and nothing to share it, no files, no windows, no way to start an app. The **operating system** (OS) is the software that turns bare hardware into something many programs and people can use at once. | Operating system | Runs on | |---|---| | Windows | most PCs | | macOS, iOS, iPadOS | Apple computers, phones, tablets | | Linux | most servers, supercomputers, many devices; Android is built on it | | Android | most phones | | Many small "real-time" systems | cars, routers, medical devices | ## Its jobs | Job | What it means | Lesson | |---|---|---| | **Run programs** | Load a program from disk into memory and start it; stop it when it ends or crashes | 6.02 | | **Share the CPU** | Switch between programs so quickly that they all seem to run at once | 6.02 | | **Share memory** | Give each program its own memory, and keep programs out of each other's | 6.03 | | **Files** | Turn a disk of numbered blocks into named files in folders | 6.04 | | **Devices** | Talk to keyboards, screens, disks, networks through **drivers**, so programs don't have to | 6.04 | | **Security** | Users, passwords, permissions: who may read which file | | | **Networking** | Send and receive data over Wi-Fi and cables | 6.06 | ## The kernel and user mode The core of the operating system is the **kernel**. It is the only code allowed to touch the hardware directly. The CPU itself enforces this with two modes: | Mode | Who runs in it | May... | |---|---|---| | **Kernel mode** (privileged) | The kernel and drivers | Do anything: any memory, any device, any instruction | | **User mode** (restricted) | Every app: your browser, a game, Python | Use only its own memory; cannot talk to devices; certain instructions cause an error | When an app needs something only the kernel may do - read a file, print, open a network connection, get more memory - it makes a **system call** (5.06): a special instruction (`syscall` on x86-64) that switches the CPU into kernel mode and jumps to a fixed entry point in the kernel. The kernel checks the request, does it, and switches back. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph User["User mode"] A1["Browser"] A2["Game"] A3["Python"] end subgraph Kernel["Kernel mode"] K["Kernel: scheduler, memory manager,
file systems, network"] D["Drivers"] end A1 -->|system calls| K A2 -->|system calls| K A3 -->|system calls| K K --> D --> HW["Hardware: CPU, memory, disk, screen, network"] ``` This separation is why one crashing app does not crash the whole computer: it can only damage its own memory, and the kernel cleans up after it. A bug in the kernel or a driver, on the other hand, can bring everything down (the Windows "blue screen"). ## What you see vs. the kernel What people usually call "the operating system" includes much more than the kernel: the desktop and windows, the file browser, settings, the command line (a **shell**), and many background services. Those are ordinary user-mode programs that come with the kernel. On Linux, the kernel is Linux itself; the rest (GNOME, KDE, the GNU tools) are separate projects packaged together into a **distribution** such as Ubuntu or Fedora. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the kernel? - The CPU's fastest core + The core of the OS, which runs the hardware - The desktop and its windows > It is the only code allowed to touch the hardware directly. Everything else runs in user mode and asks it through system calls. ? Why can an ordinary app not read the disk directly? - Apps are too slow to read disks - The disk is locked while the computer is on + In user mode the CPU forbids it > The app must ask the kernel with a system call, and the kernel checks every request, which keeps programs safe from each other. ? Why does one app crashing usually not crash the whole computer? - Apps cannot really crash - The CPU restarts automatically + Each app is kept in its own memory > The kernel stops the crashed app and cleans up; user-mode isolation contains the damage. ```
